newsitem.title: ARMENIA: IMF happy with Armenian reform, inflation a worry.
newsitem.headline: IMF happy with Armenian reform, inflation a worry.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) decision to continue lending to Armenia is a vote of support for overall reforms but higher inflation is a cause for worries, the fund's resident representative said on Wednesday.

"Our executive board was very supportive of the Armenian reform programme. This loan is to give the central bank more leverage to decide whether to intervene and whether it is necessary," Susan Jones told Reuters in an interview.

The fund approved the first $25 million tranche of a $50 million 1997 lending package on Monday, part of a larger three-year $150 million programme under the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), Jones said. $50 million was disbursed in 1996.
The IMF, complaining about poor tax collection and slow reform of the banking sector, had delayed the loan payments by several months.
Jones said the money would give "an adequate cushion to the balance of payments" and would help the country meet import and debt payments.
She said the country's better tax collection was one reasons for the loan's approval, but a higher than expected inflation rate cause for concern.
"Inflation has picked up a little more than we expected. This worries us," she said.

The government and the IMF had agreed a target year-on-year inflation rate of between 10 and 12 percent for 1997, but Jones said it had already risen 10.9 percent over the first five months of the year.
Jones said the second tranche of the 1997 package was subject to successful completion of a mid-term review to be conducted by an IMF team in October.
She said the IMF wanted to see more improvement in the tax system, continued structural changes and banking sector reforms and continued privatisation.
The government has announced open tenders for the sale of several debt-ridden large enterprises over the past few months, including a state-owned brandy plant and a lightbulb factory.
Jones said that declining exports were also a cause for concern but that it was a long-term problem, not something that could be easily rectified in the short run.
Analysts said the Armenian economy would not be able to grow to its potential unless a solution was found to the country's long-standing territorial dispute with neighbouring Azerbaijan.

The conflict over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh has closed off landlocked Armenia's traditional trade routes through Turkey and Azerbaijan, making exports more expensive and less competitive.
